findings.what: "Its third row is the sum of the first two ... That makes the column space the plane z = x + y" only proves every output lies in that plane, not that the outputs fill it, because a rank-1 matrix with the same rows rule would pass the same test; add the missing step that columns (1, 1, 2) and (1, 2, 3) do not line up, so the rank is 2 and they reach the whole plane, and drop the unexplained "with normal (−1, −1, 1)" to stay under 90 words.

findings.where: Screen 11 ("On the plane or off it"), first two sentences
findings.what: The lesson's key count arrives as the vague "Rank and null space together always account for every column", with no reason on any SHOW screen (the column-by-column reason is only in screen 13's Why? and the explain), and it shares a screen with the on-or-off-the-plane target the picture shows; state it plainly ("the rank plus the number of crushed directions is the number of columns") and add the one-line reason "each column either adds a new direction or is a mix that gives one crushed direction".

x names both the input arrow and its first number three sentences apart ("x’s first number says how much of column 1", then "an input (x, y) gives (x + 2y) lots"), which can trip him on screens 1 and 3, and the step "y lots of (2, 4) is 2y lots of (1, 2)" is skipped on the way to x + 2y.

findings.where: Screen 8 puzzle ("Must it hold the origin?")
findings.what: It tests that every column space holds the origin, which no earlier SHOW screen says; he can still reason it out and the hints cover it, but one sentence on screen 1 or 7 ("Zero lots of each column give the zero arrow, so the shaded set always passes through the origin") would make it a check rather than a leap.

findings.where: Screen 7 ("Change one number"), output panel during the demonstration
findings.what: tgtD() calls grip('b') whatever b's fade, so the dashed drag ring is drawn at (3, 7) from the first frame and sits empty on the output panel for 2.6 s before b fades in; draw the ring only once bA > 0.

Each carries 76 to 87 words in 7 to 9 sentences, all at the top of the 90-word limit, while the brief says most screens stay at one to three sentences; screens 1, 7 and 9 in particular could hand a sentence or two to the picture or the explain.

The brief promised that Matrices' no-answer ending gets its cause here, but the screen never says that this 0 = 1 is the elimination ending he already knows; the explain does, and one short sentence on the screen, traded for a weaker one, would land the payoff.

findings.where: Screen 13 ("Mixed: what it crushes"), before Check
findings.what: About 70 px of blank space sits between the four column tiles and the answer buttons at 360 px and 1280 px, kept for the brace and working line that appear after a right answer, so the picture looks unfinished before he answers.

Five footnote markers ([^1] on the column space definition, [^2] twice, [^3], [^4]) are more than "a few a lesson"; keep the ones on rules he might look up (the solution set, rank and nullity) and drop [^1] and [^3].

The four-pole RCD sentences (four inputs, one reading, three crushed directions) are a true and useful extension rather than a place where the analogy breaks, so move them into the analogy text and leave "breaks" with the phasors and the point that a one-number reading can never miss a target.
The title says "what it flattens" but no screen, hint or explain uses "flatten"; the lesson says "crushes" throughout, so one word should match the other.
